before.text:
When N ≤ T 1−ǫ we may evaluate M1 (R, T ) and M2 (R, T ) easily. These are two quadratic
forms in the unknown coefficients r(n), and the problem thus reduces to maximizing the
ratio of these quadratic forms. Solving this optimization problem we obtain Theorem 1.
   This method generalizes readily to provide large and small central values in families of
L-functions. By contrast, the method of Montgomery does not appear to generalize to this
situation. Recently Z. Rudnick and the author ([11] and [12]) found a flexible method to
obtain lower bounds for moments in many families of L-functions, but the bounds obtained
here are superior.

related_synthesis_entries.claim: In each setting, a tailored orthogonality mechanism converts a resonator norm and a central-value mixed moment into two finite quadratic forms; an unusually large or small ratio forces an extreme member of the averaging domain.
related_synthesis_entries.limit: The diagonalizing inputs differ substantially—Fourier decay in t, quadratic-character square detection, and Petersson-Hecke averaging—so the source does not establish an abstract theorem covering arbitrary families.

related_synthesis_entries.claim: The useful resonator length is set by the point at which the chosen analytic representation still suppresses off-diagonal terms; changing from a second to a fourth resonator moment or from zeta to a family changes that length budget.
related_synthesis_entries.limit: The source supplies setting-specific inequalities and does not claim these displayed length bounds are universally optimal.
